quote_json: "The identifier of a using-alias-directive must be unique within the declaration space"
notes: 1st ed 16.3.1 requires the identifier of a using-alias-directive to be unique within the declaration space of the compilation unit or namespace that immediately contains it, and calls a collision with an existing member a compile-time error (PDF p. 219 lines 36-48). The top-level declarations of every compilation unit form the single global declaration space (PDF p. 84 lines 24-25), which already holds class Record, so the top-level alias Record breaks 16.3.1, and the normative 'Likewise, it is a compile-time error' (PDF p. 219 lines 47-48) shows the rule is diagnosed. Only the 7th edition moves aliases into a separate alias declaration space that 'need not be unique within the global declaration space' (PDF p. 372 lines 32-36), so csc's acceptance belongs to the later level. The alias is never used, so no ambiguous-use error can stand in for the declaration rule, and the witness renames only the alias. Positive witnesses establish prerequisites; failing originals do not prove mutation sensitivity.

notes: 1st ed 16.3.1 requires an alias identifier to be unique within the declaration space of its immediately containing namespace, and its own example marks 'using A = N1.N2.A;' in a second N3 body, beside 'class A {}' in the first, as 'Error, A already exists' (PDF p. 219 lines 36-46). Same-named namespace declarations form one combined declaration space (PDF p. 84 lines 26-27), and the program is the edition's own erroneous example with fresh names, so a reject is required. The 7th edition permits the collision through a separate alias declaration space (PDF p. 372 lines 32-36), a later-level change. The alias is unused and the witness renames only the alias, so the test isolates the declaration rule. Positive witnesses establish prerequisites; failing originals do not prove mutation sensitivity.
